summary: Array terminology — elements, indexes, lower and upper bounds — and choosing between one- and two-dimensional arrays for a task.

blocks.content: A **fixed-size, ordered** collection of elements of the **same data type**, stored under **one identifier** and accessed by **index**.

DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER          // 1D: lower bound 1, upper bound 5
DECLARE Seats  : ARRAY[1:10, 1:20] OF CHAR       // 2D: 10 rows, 20 columns

Scores[3] ← 87
Seats[2, 15] ← 'X'

FOR i ← 1 TO 5
    OUTPUT Scores[i]
NEXT i
blocks.caption: Declaring and using arrays

blocks.title: Terms
rows: One item stored in the array

blocks.content: In many languages (Python, JavaScript, C, PHP) indexes **start at 0**: an array of length *n* has bounds **0 and n − 1**. Accessing index *n* causes a runtime **"index out of range"** error.

rows: The data is a **single list** of values
The data has **rows and columns** (a table or grid)
Several values per item, or two indexes are natural
Scores of one student; names of 30 students; daily temperatures for a month
Marks of 30 students in 6 subjects; a cinema seating plan; a chess board; temperatures per day per city

blocks.title: Choosing the structure
blocks.content:
- *Store the score of each of 25 students* → **1D** `Score[1:25]`.
- *Store the scores of 25 students in 4 tests* → **2D** `Score[1:25, 1:4]` (row = student, column = test).
- *Store a 9×9 sudoku grid* → **2D** `Grid[1:9, 1:9]`.

FOR s ← 1 TO 25
    Sum ← 0
    FOR t ← 1 TO 4
        Sum ← Sum + Score[s, t]
    NEXT t
    OUTPUT "Student ", s, " average: ", Sum / 4
NEXT s
blocks.caption: Average of each student in a 2D array

blocks.content: For a 2D array say which index is the **row** and which is the **column** — e.g. "the first index is the student, the second is the test number".
